title: Animal instinct and the riddles of Proverbs
source_text: Ἔστω δὲ καὶ ἄλλα ὑπὸ τῶν ζῴων γινώσκεσθαι ἀλεξιφάρμακα. τί οὖν τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ μὴ φύσιν ἀλλὰ λόγον εἶναι τὸν εὑρίσκοντα ταῦτα ἐν τοῖς ζῴοις; εἰ μὲν γὰρ λόγος ἦν ὁ εὑρίσκων, οὐκ ἂν ἀποτεταγμένως τόδε τι μόνον εὑρίσκετο ἐν ὄφεσιν, ἔστω καὶ δεύτερον καὶ τρίτον, καὶ ἄλλο τι ἐν ἀετῷ καὶ οὕτως ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς ζῴοις. ἀλλὰ τοσαῦτα ἂν, ὅσα καὶ ἐν ἀνθρώποις· νυνὶ δὲ φανερὸν ἐκ τοῦ ἀποτεταγμένως πρός τινα ἑκάστου φύσιν ζῴου νενευκέναι βοηθήματα ὅτι οὐ σοφία οὐδὲ λόγος ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀλλά τις φυσικὴ πρὸς τὰ τοιάδε σωτηρίας ἕνεκεν τῶν ζῴων κατασκευὴ, ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου γεγενημένη. καίτοι γε εἰ ἐβουλόμην ὁμόσε χωρεῖν τῷ Κέλσῳ κατὰ ταῦτα, ἐχρησάμην ἂν Σολομῶντος λέξει ἀπὸ τῶν Παροιμιῶν οὕτως ἐχούσῃ· „τέσσαρα δ᾿ ἐστὶν ἐλάχιστα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ταῦτα δέ ἐστι σοφώτερα τῶν σοφῶν· οἱ μύρμηκες, οἷς μὴ ἔστιν ἰσχὺς, οἳ ἑτοιμάζονται ἐν θέρει τὴν τροφήν· καὶ οἱ χοιρογρύλλιοι. ἔθνος οὐκ ἰσχυρὸν, οἳ ἐποιήσαντο ἐν πέτραις τοὺς ἑαυτῶν οἴκους· ἀβασίλευτός ἐστιν ἡ ἀκρὶς, καὶ στρατεύει ἀπὸ ἑνὸς κελεύσματος εὐτάκτως· καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδόμενος καὶ εὐάλωτος ὢν οἰκεῖ ἐν ὀχυρώμασι βασιλέως.“ ἀλλ᾿ οὐ συγχρῶμαι ὡς σαφέσι τοῖς ῥητοῖς, ἀκολούθως δὲ τῇ ἐπιγραφῇ (ἐπιγέγραπται γὰρ τὸ βιβλίον Παροιμίαι) ζητῶ ταῦτα ὡς αἰνίγματα. ἔθος γὰρ τοῖς ἀνδράσι τούτοις τὰ ἕτερον μέν τι αὐτόθεν δηλοῦντα ἕτερον δὲ ἐν ὑπονοίᾳ ἀπαγγέλλοντα διαιρεῖν εἰς εἴδη πολλὰ, ὧν (ἓν) εἶναι τὰς παροιμίας. διὸ καὶ ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις ἡμῶν γέγραπται ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν εἰρηκέναι· „ταῦτ᾿ ἐν παροιμίαις λελάληκα ὑμῖν· ἔρχεται ὥρα ὅτε οὐκέτι ἐν παροιμίαις λαλήσω ὑμῖν.“ οὐχ οἱ αἰσθητοὶ τοίνυν μύρμηκες σοφώτεροι καὶ „τῶν σοφῶν“ εἰσιν ἀλλ᾿ οἱ δηλούμενοι ὡς ἐν εἴδει παροιμιῶν. οὕτω δὲ λεκτέον καὶ περὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ζῴων· ἀλλὰ πάνυ ἁπλούστατα νομίζει εἶναι καὶ ἰδιωτικὰ ὁ Κέλσος τὰ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν βιβλία καὶ οἴεται τοὺς ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτὰ βιαζομένους τὸ βούλημα τῶν γραψάντων τοῦτο ποιεῖν. ἐληλέγχθω οὖν καὶ διὰ τούτων ὁ Κέλσος μάτην ἡμᾶς διαβάλλων· ἐληλέγχθω δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ ὁ περὶ ὄφεων καὶ ἀετῶν λόγος, ἀποφηνάμενος εἶναι τούτους ἀνθρώπων σοφωτέρους.
pass_a_gloss: Let it be that other antidotes too are known by animals. What then [is] this toward [proving] that not nature (φύσις) but reason (λόγος) is what finds these in the animals? For if reason were the finder, not in a set way (ἀποτεταγμένως) would this one thing only be found in snakes, let it be also a second and third, and some other in an eagle, and so in the remaining animals; but as many as also in men. But now [it is] plain from the fact that the aids (βοηθήματα) have inclined (νενευκέναι) in a set way toward a certain nature of each animal (πρός τινα ἑκάστου φύσιν ζῴου), that not wisdom (σοφία) nor reason is in them, but some natural constitution (φυσικὴ κατασκευή) toward such things for the sake of the safety (σωτηρία) of the animals, having come to be by the Word/Reason (ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου γεγενημένη). And yet if I wished to go to close quarters (ὁμόσε χωρεῖν) with Celsus in these, I would have used Solomon's saying (λέξις) from the Proverbs (Παροιμίαι) which runs thus: 'Four are least (ἐλάχιστα) upon the earth, and these are wiser than the wise: the ants, who have no strength, who prepare in summer their food; and the rock-hyraxes (χοιρογρύλλιοι), a nation (ἔθνος) not strong, who made in rocks their houses; kingless (ἀβασίλευτος) is the locust (ἀκρίς), and it marches (στρατεύει) from one command (κέλευσμα) in good order (εὐτάκτως); and the lizard/gecko (ἀσκαλαβώτης) supported (ἐρειδόμενος) by hands and being easily caught (εὐάλωτος) dwells in strongholds (ὀχυρώματα) of a king.' But I do not use (συγχρῶμαι) the words (ῥητά) as plain (σαφῆ), but in accordance with the title (ἐπιγραφή) (for the book is entitled Proverbs) I seek these as riddles (αἰνίγματα). For [it is] custom for these men to divide into many kinds (εἴδη) the [sayings] showing one thing directly (αὐτόθεν) and announcing another in hidden sense (ὑπόνοια), of which one is proverbs. Therefore also in our gospels it is written that our Saviour (σωτήρ) said: 'These things in proverbs I have spoken to you; an hour comes when no longer in proverbs will I speak to you.' Not therefore the sensible (αἰσθητοί) ants are wiser even than 'the wise', but those shown as in the form of proverbs. So also must be said about the remaining animals; but Celsus thinks altogether most simple (ἁπλούστατα) and unlearned (ἰδιωτικά) the books of Jews and Christians and supposes that those allegorizing (ἀλληγοροῦντες) them do this forcing (βιαζόμενοι) the intent (βούλημα) of the writers. Let Celsus then be refuted (ἐληλέγχθω) also through these, slandering us in vain; and let be refuted also his argument about snakes and eagles, having declared (ἀποφηνάμενος) these wiser than men.
pass_b_english: Suppose that other antidotes too are known to the animals. What does this do to show that it is not nature but reason that finds these things in the animals? For if reason were what found them, there would not be found in snakes, in a fixed and limited way, this one thing alone (or say a second and a third as well), and some other thing in the eagle, and so with the rest of the animals; there would be as many as are found among men. As it is, the very fact that the aids are fitted, in a fixed way, to the particular nature of each animal makes it plain that there is no wisdom or reason in them, but a natural constitution suited to such things for the preservation of the animals, a constitution made by the Word.

And yet, had I wished to meet Celsus head on in this matter, I could have used a passage of Solomon from Proverbs, which runs thus: “There are four things that are least upon the earth, but these are wiser than the wise: the ants, who have no strength, who prepare their food in summer; and the rock badgers, a people not strong, who have made their homes in the rocks; the locust has no king, and marches in good order at a single word of command; and the lizard, which leans on its hands and is easily caught, dwells in the strongholds of a king” (Proverbs 30:24–28). But I do not use these words as though their meaning were plain. In keeping with the title (for the book is entitled Proverbs), I search into them as riddles. For it is the custom of these men to divide into many kinds the sayings that show one thing on their face and announce another in a hidden sense, and one of these kinds is the proverb. That is why in our Gospels too it is written that our Saviour said: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs” (John 16:25). It is not, then, the ants we see that are wiser even “than the wise” (Proverbs 30:24), but those that are signified, as it were, in the form of proverbs. The same must be said of the other animals.

Celsus, however, thinks the books of Jews and Christians utterly simple and unlearned, and supposes that those who interpret them allegorically do so by forcing the intention of the writers. Let Celsus, then, stand refuted by these things too, as one who slanders us to no purpose; and let his argument about snakes and eagles, in which he declared them wiser than men, stand refuted as well.

choices.term: ἐκ τοῦ ... πρός τινα ἑκάστου φύσιν ζῴου νενευκέναι βοηθήματα
choices.choice: Fixed syntax of ἐκ τοῦ ... πρός τινα ἑκάστου φύσιν ζῴου νενευκέναι βοηθήματα: the aids (subject) are fitted to each animal's nature, not 'each animal's nature is bent toward particular aids'; gloss and note updated to match

'there would not be found, in a fixed way, this one thing alone among snakes' recast into natural order ('there would not be found in snakes, in a fixed and limited way, this one thing alone'), concession put in parentheses
'as many as among men' to 'as many as are found among men'
Calque 'our Saviour is written to have said' to 'it is written that our Saviour said'
John 16:25 'I shall no longer' to 'I will no longer' (no archaism)
'those signified as in the form of proverbs' to 'those that are signified, as it were, in the form of proverbs' (keeps ὡς, reads naturally)
πάνυ ἁπλούστατα: 'quite simple' to 'utterly simple' (superlative with πάνυ)
Checked Proverbs 30:24–28 against LXX wording clause by clause and John 16:25 against the Greek Gospel: both correct

Wordplay: Origen denies λόγος (reason) to the animals and then says their constitution was made ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου, by the Word (the divine Logos, maker of all). Rendered “made by the Word”, capitalised as God the Word; “by reason” is possible but loses the point. ἔστω καὶ δεύτερον καὶ τρίτον is a concession inside the sentence (“or say a second and a third as well”). In ἐκ τοῦ ἀποτεταγμένως πρός τινα ἑκάστου φύσιν ζῴου νενευκέναι βοηθήματα the subject of νενευκέναι is βοηθήματα and τινα agrees with φύσιν: the aids are bent toward (fitted to) the particular nature of each animal; rendered “the aids are fitted … to the particular nature of each animal”. Proverbs 30:24–28 is quoted in the Septuagint form; the Septuagint places this block in a different order within Proverbs (inside chapter 24 in common printed editions), so the English Bible numbering is given. LXX wording differs from the Hebrew: “wiser than the wise” (Hebrew “exceedingly wise”); χοιρογρύλλιοι = rock badgers (hyraxes, “conies”); ἀσκαλαβώτης = lizard or gecko (Hebrew śemāmît; “spider” in some English versions), rendered “lizard”; “leans on its hands and is easily caught” follows the LXX, not the Hebrew. John 16:25 matches the Gospel text; ἐν παροιμίαις kept as “in proverbs” (often “in figures of speech”) because Origen’s argument turns on the word παροιμία. “Than the wise” in the following sentence repeats Proverbs 30:24 and is cited again. ὧν (ἓν) εἶναι: Koetschau supplies ἓν; translated as supplied. “These men” (τοῖς ἀνδράσι τούτοις) refers to the scriptural writers.
